t.7.7.1: But those rākṣasa-clouds, thundering, rained down upon the mountain that was Nārāyaṇa with a shower of arrows, as clouds pour rain upon a mountain.
t.7.7.2: Viṣṇu, dark yet radiant, surrounded by those dark foremost of night-rovers, looked like a mountain of collyrium encircled by rain-pouring clouds.
t.7.7.4: So too the arrows loosed from the bows of the Rākṣasas, swift as the thunderbolt, the wind and the mind, entered into Hari, as the worlds enter into him at the close of an age.
t.7.7.3: Like locusts upon a field of grain, like mosquitoes upon a mountain, like living beings drawn to a pot of nectar, and like makaras plunging into the ocean.
t.7.7.6: The mountain-like lords of the Rākṣasas, with arrows, spears, swords and lances, left Hari unable to breathe, as breath-control does a twice-born in the practice of prāṇāyāma.
t.7.7.5: Those mounted on chariots came with their chariots, those seated on the backs of elephants with their elephants, the horsemen with their fine steeds, and the foot soldiers as well, all moving through the sky.
t.7.7.7: Assailed by the night-rangers as a mighty timi is beset by fishes, he drew his bow Śārṅga and, in that great battle, aimed at the bodies of the rākṣasas.
t.7.7.9: Having scattered that shower of arrows as the wind scatters a rising rain, Puruṣottama blew the great conch Pāñcajanya.
t.7.7.8: With arrows loosed from a bow drawn to its full length, adamant-tipped and swift as thought, Viṣṇu cut them into pieces as small as sesame seeds, by the hundreds and then by the thousands.
t.7.7.10: That water-born king of conches, blown by Hari with all his breath, roared with a terrible din, like a thundercloud at the end of a yuga.
t.7.7.11: Then that roar of the king of conches terrified the rākṣasas, as a lion, the king of beasts, terrifies rutting elephants in the forest.
t.7.7.12: The horses could not stand firm, the elephants lost their frenzy, and the warriors, enfeebled by the blast of the conch, fell from their chariots.
t.7.7.13: Released from the Śārṅga bow, the well-feathered arrows, their heads like thunderbolts, tore through those Rākṣasas and entered the earth.
t.7.7.14: And other fearsome Rākṣasas, being pierced by the arrows loosed from Nārāyaṇa's bow, fell down like mountains struck by the thunderbolt.
t.7.7.15: Through the wounds of those wound-dealing foes, wounds born of Adhokṣaja's arrows, they poured out blood in torrents, as mountains pour forth a stream of gold.
t.7.7.16: The blast of the king of conches and likewise the twang of the Śārṅga bow, the sound belonging to Viṣṇu, swallows up the cries of the rākṣasas.
t.7.7.18: Even so the arrows, loosed from Śārṅga and driven by Nārāyaṇa, sped forth swiftly as shafts by the hundreds and then by the thousands.
t.7.7.17: Like fierce rays from the sun, like waves from the ocean, like lordly serpents from a mountain, and like torrents of water from a cloud.
t.7.7.19: As lions are by a śarabha, as elephants by a lion, as tigers by an elephant, as leopards by a tiger,
t.7.7.20: Just as dogs are chased by a leopard, as cats by a dog, as snakes by a cat, and as rats by a snake…
t.7.7.21: Thus those Rākṣasas in battle, put to flight by the mighty Viṣṇu, run away, and others are laid low upon the surface of the earth.
t.7.7.22: Having slain thousands of Rākṣasas, Madhusūdana sounded his conch, just as the king of the gods makes the rain-cloud roar.
t.7.7.23: Seized by the arrows of Nārāyaṇa and utterly bewildered by the blast of his conch, the shattered rākṣasa army went back toward Laṅkā.
t.7.7.24: When the Rākṣasa army had been shattered, struck down by the arrows of Nārāyaṇa, Sumālī covered Hari in battle with a shower of arrows.
t.7.7.25: Raising his gold-adorned hand as an elephant raises its trunk, the rākṣasa roared with delight, like a rain-cloud with its lightning.
t.7.7.26: He cut off the head, with its blazing earrings, of the charioteer of the roaring Sumāli, and the horses of that Rākṣasa ran about wildly.
t.7.7.27: Sumālī, lord of the Rākṣasas, was whirled about by those bewildered horses, just as a man lacking in self-control is whirled about by the runaway horses of his senses.
t.7.7.29: Then Viṣṇu, though tormented by the arrows released by Mālin in their thousands, was not shaken in battle, just as one who has conquered his senses is not shaken by anxieties.
t.7.7.28: Mālī too rushed forward in battle, grasping his bow together with arrows. The gold-adorned arrows loosed from Mālī's bow reached Hari and entered into him, as birds enter the Krauñca mountain.
t.7.7.30: Then the blessed Lord, the sustainer of beings, bearer of sword and mace, made his bowstring twang and loosed floods of arrows against Mālin.
t.7.7.31: Those arrows, radiant as thunderbolts and lightning, reached the body of Mālin and drank his blood, as the serpents once drank the nectar of immortality.
t.7.7.33: But Mālī, foremost of the night-rangers, now deprived of his chariot, seized his mace and, mace in hand, leapt down like a lion springing from a mountain peak.
t.7.7.32: Having forcibly turned back Mālin, whose crown was adorned with a garland, Hari struck down his chariot together with its banner, his bow, and his horses.
t.7.7.34: In battle he struck Garuḍa with it on the forehead, as Antaka might strike Īśāna, or as Indra strikes a mountain with his thunderbolt.
t.7.7.35: Struck hard with a mace by that Mālin, Garuḍa, tormented by pain, turned the god away from the battle.
t.7.7.36: When the god had been made to turn his face from the battle by Mālin, through Garuḍa, a great uproar arose from the rākṣasas, who were roaring loudly.
t.7.7.37: Hearing the roar of the roaring Rākṣasas, the younger brother of Harihaya, though his face was turned away, hurled his discus, intent on slaying Mālin.
t.7.7.39: That terrifying head of the lord of the Rākṣasas, severed by the discus, fell spewing blood, just as the head of Rāhu fell long ago.
t.7.7.38: That discus, shining like the orb of the sun and resembling the wheel of Time, lit up the sky with its own radiance and struck down the head of Māli.
t.7.7.41: Seeing Mālin slain, Sumālin and Mālyavant too, together with their forces and burning with grief, ran back toward Laṅkā.
t.7.7.40: Then the gods, greatly delighted, crying out "Well done, O God!", let loose a lion's roar, uttered with all their breath.
t.7.7.42: But the high-minded Garuḍa, having recovered himself, turned back and, enraged, put the Rākṣasas to flight with the wind of his wings.
t.7.7.43: Nārāyaṇa too, with thunderbolts of excellent arrows loosed from his bow, tore apart the night-wanderers, their hair loosened and tossing, just as great Indra, attended by lightning, rends with his thunderbolts.
t.7.7.44: With its parasols shattered and its weapons falling, its bodies battered and torn apart by arrows, its entrails spilling out and its eyes darting about in fear, that army became like one gone mad.
t.7.7.45: Crushed by the Ancient Lion, the night-rangers together with their elephants raised cries and made frantic rushes all at once, like elephants tormented by a lion.
t.7.7.47: Their heads severed by blows of the discus, their limbs crushed by blows of the mace, and cut into many pieces by blows of the sword, the lords of the Rākṣasas fall like mountains.
t.7.7.46: Being covered by the nets of Hari's arrows, and loosing their own nets of arrows in return, the night-rangers, dark as storm clouds, rushed about like black clouds driven by the wind.
t.7.7.48: Their lotus-like faces were cut off by the discus, their chests crushed by the mace, their necks broken by the plough, and their heads split open by the pestles.
t.7.7.49: Some cut down by the sword, and others struck by arrows, the Rākṣasas swiftly fell from the sky into the waters of the ocean.
t.7.7.50: Then the sky was seen densely filled with night-roaming demons being struck down, their necklaces and earrings slipping away, resembling dark rain-clouds, as though dark mountains were being hurled down.
